question: Will rerunning this notebook reproduce the reported AUC of 0.874?

artifact.code:
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)
model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(roc_auc_score(y_te, model.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]))   # reported: 0.874
# No random_state is set anywhere.

ai_claim: Yes. The same code and data produce the same model and the same AUC every time.

ai_solution.text: The code is unchanged.
The data are unchanged.
The same inputs produce the same outputs.
So the AUC is 0.874 again.

failure.explanation: train_test_split shuffles randomly and the random forest bootstraps and samples features randomly. Without random_state, each run uses a different split and different trees, so the AUC changes (e.g. 0.861-0.883). Set random_state (and record library versions) for reproducibility, and report variation across seeds.

canonical_solution: No: the split and the forest are random without seeds. Set random_state and report results across several seeds.
counterexamples: A colleague rerunning the notebook gets a different number.

hints.text: Find the random steps in the code.
Step 3 assumes the same inputs give the same outputs.
Randomised algorithms need fixed seeds to be reproducible.
Run the cell twice.
Step 3 is wrong: random steps are unseeded. Set random_state.

repair: Set random_state in the split and the model; record package versions.
debrief: Reproducibility is a prerequisite for trusting and comparing results. Seeds, versions and data snapshots all need recording.

question: Will the deployed model perform like its offline AUC of 0.88?

artifact.code:
# Training (batch SQL): avg_order_value_30d = AVG(order_value) over the last 30 days, excluding cancelled orders.
# Serving (API code): avg_order_value_30d = mean of the last 30 orders, including cancelled ones.
# Offline validation AUC: 0.88

ai_claim: Yes. The feature has the same name and meaning in training and serving, so the model receives the same inputs and performs as validated.

ai_solution.text: Both pipelines compute avg_order_value_30d.
The feature has the same name in both.
So the model receives the same feature in production.
Production AUC will be about 0.88.

failure.misconception: Computing a feature differently in training and serving
failure.explanation: The two implementations differ: 30 days versus 30 orders, and cancelled orders excluded versus included. The model learned relationships for one definition and receives values from another - training-serving skew - so production performance can fall well below 0.88. Compute features with one shared implementation (a feature store or shared library), and log served features to compare with training.
failure.why_convincing: Same name, same intent, so it seems the same feature.

canonical_solution: No: the serving feature differs in window and filtering, so the model sees different inputs. Share one feature implementation.

valid_evidence.summary: Training uses 30 days excluding cancellations; serving uses 30 orders including them.
For a sample of customers, served values differ from training values by more than 20% in 35% of cases.

counterexamples: A customer with many cancelled orders gets a different feature value online.

hints.text: Compare the two definitions line by line.
Step 3 assumes the same name means the same computation.
Training-serving skew arises when features are computed differently.
Compare served and training values for the same customer.
Step 3 is wrong: the definitions differ. Use one implementation.

repair: Use a shared feature pipeline (feature store) and monitor served-versus-training feature distributions.
debrief: A model is only as good as the consistency of its inputs. Two implementations of one feature will drift apart.

subject: machine-learning
subtopic: A final test set used once
question: Is the AI right that 0.846 is an unbiased estimate of the final model's performance on similar new data?

artifact.process:
1. Split off a 15% test set and do not touch it.
2. Do all feature work, model selection and tuning with cross-validation on the remaining 85%.
3. Fit the chosen pipeline on the 85% and score it once on the test set: AUC 0.846.

ai_claim: Yes. No decision was made using the test set, so the single final score is an unbiased estimate for new data drawn from the same distribution.

ai_solution.text: The test set was held out before any work began.
All selection and tuning used cross-validation on the other 85%.
The final pipeline was scored on the test set exactly once.
No choice depended on the test set, so its score is unbiased.

canonical_solution: Correct. A test set untouched by any decision gives an unbiased (if noisy) estimate. It is unbiased for data like the test set; distribution shift in production is a separate question.

valid_evidence.summary: The test set was scored once, after all choices were fixed.

hints.text: Check whether any decision used the test set.
Step 4 depends on the test set being used only once.
An untouched test set gives an unbiased estimate.
Trace every decision to the data it used.
This solution is correct. The test set was used once at the end. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: The discipline is simple and often broken: decide everything first, then look at the test set once.

subject: machine-learning
question: Will monthly retraining keep the model's accuracy close to its launch level?

artifact.plan: Retrain the demand-forecasting model on the first of every month using the latest 24 months of data.
artifact.unknown: How quickly the relationship between features and demand changes has not been measured.

ai_claim: Yes. Retraining every month keeps the model up to date, so its accuracy stays close to the launch level.

ai_solution.text: The model is retrained every month.
Each retraining uses the latest data.
So the model is always up to date.
Accuracy stays near the launch level.

missing_information: How fast the data drift. If patterns change slowly, monthly retraining is plenty; if they shift within weeks (flash sales, a new competitor, a sudden event), accuracy can fall between retrainings - and 24 months of mostly old data may dilute recent changes. Drift has not been measured.
resolving_scenarios: Demand patterns change gradually over quarters: monthly retraining keeps accuracy near launch level.
A competitor launch changes buying patterns within two weeks: accuracy drops sharply mid-month, and the 24-month window adapts slowly.
canonical_solution: It depends on the rate and nature of drift, which is unknown. Step 3 assumes monthly updates are frequent enough.

valid_evidence.summary: After a sudden market change, error could double within two weeks, before the next scheduled retrain.

counterexamples: Fast drift can outpace a monthly schedule.

hints.text: Ask how quickly the data change.
Step 3 assumes monthly is often enough.
Retraining frequency should follow measured drift and performance decay.
Consider a sudden change mid-month.
Step 3 assumes slow drift. With slow drift it works; with fast drift it does not. It cannot be decided.

repair: Measure performance decay over time (backtests), monitor drift, and trigger retraining on alerts as well as on schedule.
debrief: Retraining schedules are hypotheses about drift. Backtesting accuracy over time tells you how often a model actually needs refreshing.
